power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background & Aims: Most prognostic models for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) target prespecified hepatic endpoints, potentially limiting attainable accuracy.
text.formatted: Background & Aims: Most prognostic models for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) target prespecified hepatic endpoints, potentially limiting attainable accuracy.

text.text: We developed and externally validated a model that learns the future hepatic phenotype most reliably predictable from baseline clinical characteristics.
Methods: We analyzed 332 HALO-MASLD participants (456 follow-up observations).
Sparse Canonical Outcome REgression (SCORE) learned a weighted phenotype from eight hepatic measures, coupled with broken adaptive ridge regression using 99 baseline predictor columns.

Participant-level nested five-fold cross-validation compared prediction of the learned phenotype with future liver stiffness measurement (LSM), controlled attenuation parameter (CAP), and FIB-4 benchmarks.
Models were externally validated without refitting in the independent NIDDK NAFLD Adult Database 2 cohort (520 participants, 732 follow-up observations).
Biological validity and bootstrap stability were also assessed.
Results: The learned phenotype emphasized lower platelet count and higher bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and LSM.
In HALO, predictive correlation was r = 0.860 (95% CI [0.824, 0.896]) and predictive R² = 0.671, versus r = 0.763 for LSM and r = 0.469 for CAP predicted from all baseline variables.
All six prespecified comparisons remained significant after Holm correction (p Holm < 0.05).
text.formatted: All six prespecified comparisons remained significant after Holm correction (p Holm < 0.05).

text.text: The phenotype correlated with MRE stiffness (ρ = 0.694) and biopsy fibrosis stage (ρ = 0.567), and was higher with imaging evidence of portal hypertension (p < 0.001).
text.formatted: The phenotype correlated with MRE stiffness (ρ = 0.694) and biopsy fibrosis stage (ρ = 0.567), and was higher with imaging evidence of portal hypertension (p < 0.001).

text.text: Bootstrap relearning yielded mean phenotype correlation 0.947.
In NIDDK, predictive correlation was r = 0.836 (95% CI [0.805, 0.863]; predictive R² = 0.680), and associations with fibrosis and portal hypertension replicated.
Conclusions: Learning the prediction target produced a sparse, clinically interpretable hepatic phenotype more accurately predicted than conventional longitudinal MASLD endpoints in both cohorts.
The resulting LIFT-MASLD model is available at https://liftmasld.github.io.
text.formatted: The resulting LIFT-MASLD model is available at <ref type="url" target="https://liftmasld.github.io">https://liftmasld.github.io</ref>.

text.text: Conventional prognostic models for MASLD target prespecified endpoints, although no single marker fully captures future hepatic disease severity.

We instead learned a multivariate hepatic phenotype optimized for longitudinal prediction and identified a sparse composite that was predicted more accurately than future liver stiffness or CAP in both development and external validation cohorts.

The learned phenotype was also associated with independent measures of fibrosis and portal hypertension that were not targeted during outcome learning, demonstrating that improved predictability could be achieved while retaining clinical relevance.

By forecasting this clinically meaningful hepatic state from a small set of routinely collected baseline measurements, LIFT-MASLD offers clinicians a new approach to longitudinal monitoring and provides researchers with a framework for developing more predictable, biologically meaningful prognostic outcomes.

Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is the most common chronic liver disease worldwide and spans a broad spectrum from steatosis to steatohepatitis, progressive fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma (European Association for the Study of the Liver et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is the most common chronic liver disease worldwide and spans a broad spectrum from steatosis to steatohepatitis, progressive fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma (European Association for the Study of the <ref type="bibr">Liver et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Approximately onethird of the global adult population has steatotic liver disease, and prevalence continues to increase (Riazi et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Approximately onethird of the global adult population has steatotic liver disease, and prevalence continues to increase <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Riazi et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: However, the clinical course of MASLD is highly heterogeneous.
Many individuals remain stable for years, whereas others progress to advanced fibrosis, portal hypertension, hepatic decompensation, or liver-related death (Sanyal et al., 2021a).
text.formatted: Many individuals remain stable for years, whereas others progress to advanced fibrosis, portal hypertension, hepatic decompensation, or liver-related death <ref type="bibr">(Sanyal et al., 2021a)</ref>.

text.text: Identifying which patients will develop clinically consequential disease therefore remains a central challenge.

Fibrosis has accordingly become a central focus of MASLD risk stratification because histologic fibrosis stage strongly predicts liver-related morbidity and mortality (Ekstedt et al., 2015; Angulo et al., 2015; Sanyal et al., 2021a).
text.formatted: Fibrosis has accordingly become a central focus of MASLD risk stratification because histologic fibrosis stage strongly predicts liver-related morbidity and mortality <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Ekstedt et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Angulo et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Sanyal et al., 2021a)</ref>.

text.text: Clinical pathways therefore aim first to identify patients with advanced fibrosis, commonly beginning with the fibrosis-4 index (FIB-4), a blood-based score derived from age, aminotransferases, and platelet count, followed when indicated by imaging-based assessment of liver stiffness (European Association for the Study of the Liver et al., 2024; Shah et al., 2009).

text.text: Prediction studies have then similarly focused on prespecified fibrosis-related targets, including future progression to fibrosis (Ghandian et al., 2022), liverstiffness or histologic fibrosis progression (Zhou et al., 2026), and classification of histologic fibrosis stage (Chang et al., 2023).

text.text: Thus, although predictor models have become increasingly sophisticated, the clinical outcome to be predicted is generally specified in advance.
Fibrosis, however, does not capture the entire hepatic disease state.

Clinicians routinely consider other measures such as platelet count, bilirubin, albumin, and evidence of portal hypertension, which reflect complementary aspects of hepatic function and disease severity.

Fibrosis measurements are also imperfect: liver biopsy samples only a small fraction of the liver and exhibits substantial sampling variability (Ratziu et al., 2005), while transient elastography measures stiffness as a surrogate for fibrosis and can disagree with histologic staging (Myers et al., 2010).

text.text: Consequently, a prespecified fibrosis-related endpoint may capture only part of the clinically relevant future disease state and may contain measurement error and biological variability that impose an intrinsic limit on predictive accuracy (Lundberg et al., 2024).

text.text: Improving longitudinal prediction may therefore require optimizing not only the predictor model but also the clinical state being predicted.

We therefore sought to develop an accurate longitudinal prediction model of future hepatic status in MASLD by jointly optimizing the prediction model and the clinical outcome being predicted, while ensuring that the learned outcome retains a clear clinical interpretation.

To this end, we employed Sparse Canonical Outcome REgression (SCORE), which learns an interpretable weighted combination of clinically meaningful outcomes that maximizes prospective predictability from baseline characteristics (Strobl, 2025).
text.formatted: To this end, we employed Sparse Canonical Outcome REgression (SCORE), which learns an interpretable weighted combination of clinically meaningful outcomes that maximizes prospective predictability from baseline characteristics <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Strobl, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: We applied SCORE to eight hepatic measures spanning steatosis, liver stiffness, biochemical function and injury, and platelet count, together with sparse predictor selection.

We hypothesized that this approach would yield a clinically meaningful hepatic phenotype that could be predicted more accurately and consistently over time than conventional endpoints, while also being associated with independent measures of fibrosis and advanced liver disease.
We finally evaluated the generalizability of the trained prediction model in an independent cohort.

Data were obtained from the University of Pittsburgh Health Assessments and Longitudinal Outcomes in MASLD (HALO-MASLD) study, a prospective longitudinal cohort designed to characterize risk factors and biomarkers associated with MASLD progression.
The parent cohort recruited adults aged 18-79 years with diagnosed MASLD through the University of Pittsburgh/UPMC liver program and affiliated research recruitment pathways.

Participants underwent detailed annual assessments of hepatic and systemic health, including transient elastography, anthropometric and body-composition measurements, laboratory testing, medication and comorbidity assessment, patient-reported outcomes, lifestyle measures, and biospecimen collection.

For the present study, we included participants with MASLD who had baseline clinical characteristics available at the first study visit and hepatic outcome measurements available at the second and/or third visits.
Measurements obtained at the first visit were used exclusively as predictors, whereas measurements obtained at subsequent visits were used to define and evaluate prospective hepatic outcomes.
The HALO-MASLD study was approved by the University of Pittsburgh Institutional Review Board (STUDY 21030003).
The study was conducted in accordance with the ethical principles of the Declaration of Helsinki, and all participants provided written informed consent before participation.
The present analysis was separately reviewed by the University of Pittsburgh IRB and determined not to constitute human subjects research (STUDY26100015).
We developed a longitudinal clinical prediction model to predict hepatic status at subsequent study visits from clinical characteristics measured at baseline.

We restricted the primary analysis to eight prespecified hepatic outcomes chosen to capture complementary dimensions of MASLD severity: controlled attenuation parameter (CAP) for steatosis, FibroScan liver stiffness measurement (LSM) for fibrosis-related stiffness, total bilirubin and albumin for hepatic function, alkaline phosphatase, aspartate aminotransferase (AST), and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) for biochemical injury, and platelet count as a marker associated with advanced fibrosis and portal hypertension.

We excluded broader patient-reported measures, such as PROMIS domains, from the primary outcome set because they reflect general physical and psychological health rather than hepatic disease specifically (Cella et al., 2010).
text.formatted: We excluded broader patient-reported measures, such as PROMIS domains, from the primary outcome set because they reflect general physical and psychological health rather than hepatic disease specifically <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Cella et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: We constructed the predictor matrix exclusively from measurements obtained at the first visit.

The resulting matrix contained 99 predictor columns spanning demographic characteristics, anthropometric and body-composition measurements, baseline liver measurements, metabolic laboratory values, comorbidities, medications, lifestyle characteristics, family history, and indicators of missing measurements.
We provide the comprehensive list of variables in Appendix Table 4.

text.text: Sex was defined as sex assigned at birth and encoded as a binary indicator for male sex.
We log-transformed selected right-skewed laboratory and elastography variables before analysis.
Missing predictor values were median-imputed using medians estimated exclusively within each training sample.
Follow-up observations were included in the primary analysis only when all eight hepatic outcomes were observed; follow-up outcomes were not imputed.
We oriented outcomes such that larger values represented greater hepatic disease burden and therefore reversed albumin and platelet count before scaling.
Within each training sample, outcomes were min-max scaled and the predictor and outcome matrices were centered separately within each follow-up visit.
We used SCORE to determine the multivariate hepatic phenotype that could be most accurately predicted from baseline characteristics.
Let Y t denote the matrix of hepatic outcomes measured at follow-up visit t and X t the corresponding baseline predictor matrix.

SCORE learns a nonnegative outcome-weight vector α together with visit-specific predictor vectors β t by maximizing predictive dependence between the learned phenotype Y t α and its baseline prediction X t β t across follow-up visits (Strobl, 2025): where q = 8 was the number of candidate hepatic outcomes.

text.text: SCORE alternates between updating the predictor coefficients β t conditional on the current outcome weights and updating α conditional on the current predictor model.
To obtain a highly parsimonious clinical prediction model, we replaced the predictor-side ordinary least-squares step with broken adaptive ridge (BAR) regression (Dai et al., 2018).
text.formatted: To obtain a highly parsimonious clinical prediction model, we replaced the predictor-side ordinary least-squares step with broken adaptive ridge (BAR) regression <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Dai et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: BAR uses iterative reweighted L 2 penalties to approximate L 0 regularization, which penalizes the number of nonzero coefficients rather than continuously shrinking their magnitudes.
This typically yields sparser solutions than L 1 regularization while reducing shrinkage of retained predictors.
Conditional on α, BAR repeatedly solved weighted ridge regressions of Y t α on X t .
At iteration m, where λ denotes the BAR penalty and ϵ is a numerical stabilization constant.
We optimized SCORE from multiple initial values to reduce sensitivity to local optima.
During crossvalidation, we used three starting values for each candidate λ.
After selecting λ, we used 10 starting values for the final fit and retained the solution with the largest SCORE objective.
We considered 15 logarithmically spaced values of λ between 10 -4 and 10 0 .

Predictive performance was estimated using five-fold nested cross-validation with folds defined at the participant level, such that all observations from the same participant remained in either the training or test sample.
Within each outer training fold, we performed five-fold inner cross-validation to select λ.

The hepatic phenotype and corresponding predictor model were independently learned within each inner training sample, and λ was selected to maximize out-of-sample correlation between the observed phenotype and its prediction from baseline characteristics.
We then refit SCORE-BAR on the complete outer training sample using the selected λ and evaluated the resulting clinical prediction model in the untouched outer test subjects.

After estimating predictive performance, we selected the final BAR penalty by maximizing mean innercross-validation performance across the outer training folds and refit SCORE-BAR using all eligible observations.
This final fit was used to characterize the learned outcome weights, selected baseline predictors, and associations of the learned phenotype with independent measures of liver disease.
We compared the predictive accuracy of the learned clinical prediction model with models targeting two conventional longitudinal MASLD endpoints: future FibroScan LSM and future CAP.
For both endpoints, we first fitted BAR using the complete baseline predictor panel.

For future LSM, we additionally evaluated baseline LSM alone, baseline FIB-4 alone, baseline FIB-4 combined with baseline LSM, and a clinical model containing baseline LSM, age, sex, body mass index, type 2 diabetes, and ALT.
The clinical model was fitted using both ordinary linear regression and BAR.

For future CAP, we evaluated baseline CAP alone and a clinical model containing baseline CAP, age, sex, body mass index, type 2 diabetes, and triglycerides, again using both ordinary linear regression and BAR.
The same participant-level outer folds were used for all comparisons.
We externally validated the trained models using the independent National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK) NAFLD Adult Database 2 cohort (Sanyal et al., 2021b).

We applied the final SCORE-BAR model trained on the complete HALO cohort to NIDDK without refitting or recalibration.
The learned phenotype was calculated using the original HALO outcome weights and min-max scaling parameters.

Because albumin, AST, and ALT received zero weights in the final learned phenotype, we required complete follow-up measurements only for the five outcomes with nonzero weights: CAP, LSM, total bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and platelet count.
The resulting external-validation sample contained 732 follow-up observations.
Baseline predictors were harmonized to the HALO definitions, and missing values were imputed using the original HALO training medians.
For comparison, we similarly applied the conventional prediction benchmarks trained on HALO, including the final BAR models for future CAP and LSM using the complete HALO baseline predictor panel.
These models retained their original selected predictors, regression coefficients, calibration parameters, and preprocessing transformations.

Predictors unavailable in identical form were harmonized where possible; in particular, the HALO cirrhosis diagnosis indicator was approximated using baseline imaging and centrally reviewed histologic evidence of cirrhosis in NIDDK.
No model parameters were re-estimated.
We evaluated predictive performance using Pearson correlation, normalized root mean squared error (NRMSE), and predictive R² .

In HALO, Pearson correlations were calculated separately within each outer crossvalidation fold and follow-up visit, transformed using Fisher's z transformation, and combined using weights proportional to the corresponding sample size minus three.

Prediction errors were normalized by the observed outcome standard deviation within each fold and visit, and NRMSE was calculated by taking the square root of the mean squared standardized errors pooled across all follow-up observations.

Predictive R² was defined as i∈It (z it -z t ) 2 , where z it and ˆ︁ z it denote the observed and predicted values of the model-specific outcome for participant i at follow-up visit t, respectively, I t denotes the participants observed at visit t, and z t denotes the corresponding observed outcome mean.
Thus, predictive R² quantified the reduction in squared prediction error relative to visit-specific mean prediction.
All three metrics combined observations across visits rather than taking an unweighted average of visit-specific performance.
In NIDDK, the same aggregation principles were used, except that correlations and prediction-error normalization were calculated within follow-up visits without cross-validation fold stratification.
Each model was evaluated against its designated outcome.
We quantified uncertainty in HALO predictive performance using 2,000 participant-level bootstrap resamples of the out-of-fold predictions generated by nested cross-validation.
Participants were resampled so that repeated visits remained together.

Predictive performance was recalculated without retraining the models in order to isolate sampling variability in performance evaluation from variability in model estimation (Tsamardinos et al., 2018).

For pairwise comparisons, the same bootstrap sample was applied to both sets of out-of-fold predictions and differences in each performance metric were calculated within each replicate.

We used 10,000 participantlevel bootstrap resamples for the prespecified comparisons of the learned clinical prediction model with BAR prediction of future LSM using the complete baseline predictor panel and with prediction of future LSM using baseline FIB-4 alone, across all three performance metrics.
Two-sided bootstrap p-values were calculated by comparing the observed differences with the centered bootstrap distributions, using a finite-sample correction.

We selected the former comparator because it used the full set of available baseline predictors while retaining future LSM as the prespecified outcome, and the latter because FIB-4 is widely used as a first-line clinical tool for fibrosis risk stratification in MASLD.
The resulting six p-values were adjusted using the Holm procedure.
The same paired participant-resampling approach was used for comparisons in NIDDK.
We evaluated persistence of predictive accuracy across follow-up intervals using the signed change in out-ofsample correlation, ∆ = r visit 3 -r visit 2 .
Values near zero indicated stable predictive performance, whereas negative values indicated lower predictive accuracy at visit 3.
We obtained 95% confidence intervals for visit-specific correlations and their changes using 2,000 participant-level bootstrap resamples in both HALO and NIDDK.
We evaluated the clinical interpretation of the learned hepatic phenotype using complementary measures of liver disease severity available in subsets of participants.

We prioritized MRE liver stiffness and histologic fibrosis stage as established measures of fibrotic disease, and imaging evidence of portal hypertension as a clinically consequential manifestation of advanced liver disease.
Each measure was matched to the corresponding follow-up visit.
Associations with continuous or ordinal measures were quantified using Spearman rank correlation to allow for monotonic but potentially nonlinear relationships.
For binary imaging evidence of portal hypertension, we compared mean learned phenotype values between participants with and without portal hypertension.
We obtained 95% confidence intervals and two-sided p-values using 10,000 participant-level bootstrap resamples, with p-values calculated from centered bootstrap distributions.
We repeated these analyses in NIDDK using centrally reviewed histologic fibrosis stage and imaging evidence of portal hypertension.

Histologic fibrosis stages were harmonized to a common ordinal scale, and imaging evidence of portal hypertension was defined by documented splenomegaly, ascites, or other portal-hypertension features on abdominal ultrasound, CT, or MRI.
These measures were matched to the corresponding follow-up visit.
The same participant-level bootstrap procedures were applied.
Quantitative MRE stiffness measurements were unavailable in NIDDK.
We assessed reproducibility of the model-defined phenotype using 200 participant-level bootstrap samples.
For each replicate, we resampled participants with replacement and repeated five-fold cross-validation over the original 15-value λ grid using three SCORE starting values for each candidate λ.
We then relearned the first hepatic phenotype using the selected λ and 10 starting values, thereby incorporating variability arising from participant sampling, BAR tuning, and SCORE optimization.
We quantified stability of the outcome weights using cosine similarity between the bootstrap estimate ˆ︁ α (b) and the original estimate ˆ︁ α.

We separately quantified stability of the resulting phenotype using a common reference outcome matrix Y ref , containing the pooled follow-up observations after outcome orientation and min-max scaling, without visit centering.
For each bootstrap replicate, we calculated the correlation between b) and Y ref ˆ︁ α.
Both quantities were summarized using their means and 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles.

We developed and both internally and externally validated a sparse clinical prediction model for future hepatic status in MASLD.

Rather than prespecifying a single longitudinal marker as the prediction target, the model used SCORE to identify the multivariate hepatic phenotype that could be predicted most reliably from baseline clinical characteristics.

The resulting phenotype emphasized lower platelet count, higher bilirubin, higher alkaline phosphatase, and greater liver stiffness and was predicted more accurately than conventional future LSM or CAP in both the HALO and NIDDK cohorts.

Predictive accuracy remained high across follow-up visits, while independent biological validation in both cohorts supported the construct validity of the learned phenotype as a clinically meaningful measure of advanced liver disease.
The results suggest that the choice of prediction target can be as important as the choice of prediction algorithm.
Most clinical prognostic models prespecify a marker such as liver stiffness or fibrosis stage and then seek to improve performance by adding predictors or increasing model flexibility.
Prediction, however, remains constrained by the intrinsic predictability and measurement properties of that target.

In the present study, allowing the clinical prediction model to learn a multivariate target produced a future hepatic state that could be predicted substantially more accurately from baseline information.
This strategy is consistent with task-aligned outcome learning, in which the most useful outcome representation may depend on the inferential goal (Strobl, 2026).
text.formatted: This strategy is consistent with task-aligned outcome learning, in which the most useful outcome representation may depend on the inferential goal <ref type="bibr">(Strobl, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: It does not replace conventional fibrosis endpoints when fibrosis itself is the clinical question, but offers a complementary strategy when the objective is accurate prospective prediction of overall hepatic disease severity.
The phenotype learned by the model was clinically coherent.
Platelet count received the greatest weight, followed by bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and LSM, whereas CAP, AST, and ALT received little or no weight.

Its associations with MRE liver stiffness, histologic fibrosis stage, and evidence of portal hypertension supported the construct validity of the learned composite outcome as a clinically meaningful representation of advanced liver disease, even though these measures were not explicitly targeted during outcome learning.

This interpretation was further supported by independent replication in NIDDK, where the phenotype was associated with centrally reviewed histologic fibrosis stage and was significantly higher among patients with imaging evidence of portal hypertension.
The predictor model was also highly sparse: only six of the 99 baseline predictor columns received nonzero coefficients, requiring just five routinely collected clinical measurements.
Thus, the model provides interpretability on both sides of the prediction task: what clinical state is being predicted and which baseline measurements are used to predict it.
We refer to the final prediction model as LIFT-MASLD (Liver Integrated Forecasting Tool for MASLD) and have implemented it as a web-based calculator at https://liftmasld.github.io.

text.text: These properties suggest potential applications in clinical monitoring and precision medicine.

For example, a patient with modest baseline liver stiffness but low platelet count and elevated bilirubin might have a relatively high predicted LIFT-MASLD value, indicating greater anticipated hepatic disease burden than liver stiffness alone would suggest.
Such predictions could complement conventional assessments when monitoring patients longitudinally.

More broadly, LIFT-MASLD could be incorporated into a patient digital twin framework integrating computational predictions with experimental measurements from patient-derived liver microphysiological systems (Miedel et al., 2025).
text.formatted: More broadly, LIFT-MASLD could be incorporated into a patient digital twin framework integrating computational predictions with experimental measurements from patient-derived liver microphysiological systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Miedel et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Comparing predicted hepatic status with disease characteristics and drug responses measured in patient-derived liver MPS could help connect clinical forecasts to underlying biological mechanisms and support the development of personalized therapeutic strategies.
Several limitations should be considered.

First, the prediction model uses a linear predictor structure; nonlinear approaches could potentially capture additional interactions, although the present formulation offers interpretability and sparsity.

Second, the analysis included only two subsequent follow-up visits, and longer follow-up will be needed to determine whether the model-defined phenotype correlates with other clinical outcomes such as hepatic decompensation, hepatocellular carcinoma, transplantation, or liver-related mortality.

Third, although the model was externally validated in the independent NIDDK cohort, HALO was a single-center cohort that was predominantly White, and additional validation across diverse populations and clinical settings would further establish transportability.
Finally, the predictors were primarily routinely available clinical, laboratory, anthropometric, and imaging variables; molecular measurements may provide additional predictive information.
In conclusion, we developed and externally validated a sparse clinical prediction model for longitudinal hepatic status in MASLD.
By allowing the prediction target itself to be learned, the model identified a clinically meaningful hepatic phenotype with independent evidence of construct validity.
This phenotype was more accurately predicted than conventional future LSM or CAP in both cohorts, using only a small set of routinely collected baseline clinical measurements.
